report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 69 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Background.
Rule-derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce.
Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration.
We ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on Escherichia coli urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW.
The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern).
Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits.

Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or priorprobability correction.
These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training.
Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history.
UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model.
Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patientcluster bootstrap intervals.
All rule-derived labels were susceptible.

Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary.
The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline.
Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries.
Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5.
The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses).
At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration.
Conclusions.
Under these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training.
Evaluations of weak supervision should include such a baseline and should report calibration as well as discrimination.
Supervised models need labelled examples, and labels are often the expensive part of a machine learning project.
Weak supervision replaces part of the manual labelling with cheaper sources such as heuristic rules, knowledge bases or other imperfect labellers.
Snorkel made this approach practical by letting users write labelling functions and combining their noisy outputs without ground-truth labels [1].

The WRENCH benchmark was built because these methods had been evaluated on different, often private, datasets with different weak sources and evaluation protocols, which made results hard to compare [2].

text.text: Our study asks a related question in a different setting.
When a fixed number of reported labels is available, is it better to keep some for choosing how rule-derived labels are used, or to train a reported-only model on all of them?
Zhu et al.'s findings motivate this comparison; they do not show what will happen in tabular clinical microbiology data.
Weak labels are also not uniformly useful.

In an empirical study of generative models trained with weak supervision, Hernández-González and Pérez found that weakly labelled data helped when fully labelled data were limited, and that the benefit depended on how much supervision information the weak labels carried and how informative it was [6].

text.text: Rule-derived labels in our setting carry a particular kind of information: the rules we study only ever imply susceptibility, so every added label belongs to the majority class.
Adding labels from one class changes the class balance of the training data, and class balance affects predicted probabilities.
In clinical risk prediction, corrections for class imbalance such as undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE did not improve discrimination and produced badly miscalibrated risks [7].

text.text: Rulederived labels need not satisfy this assumption, because they are attached to cultures that were selected differently from those with reported results.
Antimicrobial susceptibility data provide a natural test case.

The Stanford Antibiotic Resistance Microbiology Dataset (ARMD) releases reported susceptibility results and, separately, implied susceptibility labels inferred by linking results between related antibiotics according to Stanford microbiology laboratory protocols based on CLSI standards [12].

text.text: In UT Southwestern data, weak labels therefore have to be constructed by the researcher, and their validity for that laboratory cannot be assumed.
We compare reported-only training with several ways of adding rule-derived labels at fixed reported-label budgets, at both sites.
The main comparator is an all-budget reported-only baseline that spends the whole budget on training.
This is an empirical comparison of established techniques, not a new algorithm.
The UT Southwestern analysis refits the models on UT Southwestern data with a different feature set and differently constructed labels.
It is therefore an exploratory independent-site replication of the design, not an external validation of a fixed Stanford-trained model in the sense used in prediction-model research [14].

text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: We used two publicly released, de-identified microbiology datasets derived from electronic health records: Stanford ARMD (dataset release of 22 October 2025) [12] and ARMD-UTSW (Dryad version of 26 September 2025) [13].
text.formatted: We used two publicly released, de-identified microbiology datasets derived from electronic health records: Stanford ARMD (dataset release of 22 October 2025) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> and ARMD-UTSW (Dryad version of 26 September 2025) <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: From each, we used the culture cohort, demographic and prior-resistance files.
At Stanford we also used the released impliedsusceptibility file.
The unit of analysis was a culture order, identified by the composite key of patient, encounter and order identifiers, all read as strings.
We selected E. coli urine cultures with a complete key.
At UT Southwestern, culture orders linked to more than one patient or encounter would have been excluded; none were found.
The outcome for each target antibiotic was reported non-susceptibility: Resistant or Intermediate = 1, Susceptible = 0.
Other reported values (for example, inconclusive) were ignored, and a culture whose valid reported results disagreed on the binary outcome was excluded.
The organism is treated as known, so the task is not prediction of the organism before culture.
Target antibiotics were cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime at Stanford, and cefepime and ceftazidime in the UT Southwestern modelling experiment.
UT Southwestern cefoxitin was audited but not modelled: it had 56 reported cultures with 3 non-susceptible results, below the prespecified minimum of 50 cultures per class.
Stanford.
We used the released implied-susceptibility labels as provided, applying the same binary mapping.
Keys with conflicting implied labels, keys that did not match an E. coli urine culture, and keys that also had a reported result for the target were excluded.
All released implied labels for these targets were susceptible.
We applied the E. coli rules from the Stanford rule file as research weaklabelling heuristics.
Cefepime and ceftazidime: susceptible if susceptible to ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or cefazolin.
Cefoxitin: susceptible if susceptible to cefazolin.
These are Stanford laboratory reporting rules.
They were not independently validated for UT Southwestern, and we do not present them as UT Southwestern labels or as rules suitable for patient care.
We used a conservative version fixed before training.

A culture received a weak susceptible label only if at least one source antibiotic was reported susceptible, no source antibiotic was reported non-susceptible, and no source antibiotic had conflicting results on that culture.
Cultures with any reported result for the target received no weak label.
Missing results never produced a label.
As a diagnostic, rule predictions were compared with reported target results on cultures that had both.
These cultures were selected for testing of both drugs, so agreement on them may not carry over to the cultures that receive weak labels.
While preparing the UT Southwestern analysis, we checked whether the rule text reproduces Stanford's released labels.
Applying the cefoxitin rule (susceptible to cefazolin, no reported cefoxitin result) to Stanford E. coli urine cultures gave 24,217 cultures.
Of these, 18,123 had a released Stanford implied label and 6,094 did not.
The released labels therefore reflect conditions beyond the rule text, and labels derived from the same text at UT Southwestern are not equivalent to them.

Stanford primary features: age band; gender code (an unordered category; no meaning is given to the codes); ordering mode; and, for any resistance, resistance to the target antibiotic and E. coli resistance, the number of prior-resistance records, the smallest day offset and the number of records within 30, 90 and 365 days (log1p-transformed; no history encoded as 0 records and 99,999 days).
Positive values of `resistant_time_to_culturetime` were read as days before the culture, and zero, negative and non-numeric offsets were excluded.
Neither the direction of this offset nor when earlier results became available is independently verified.
UT Southwestern primary features: age band only.
Gender was excluded because its coding is not known to match Stanford's.

The UT Southwestern documentation does not describe an ordering-mode field, and it describes the history offset only as days between the culture order and the susceptibility result, which does not establish its direction or availability.
A reported-only sensitivity analysis added history features under the Stanford assumption; it is reported in the exported results but not used for the main comparisons.
Because the feature sets differ, absolute performance is not comparable between sites.
Identifiers, the current result, label source, rule provenance and same-culture results for other antibiotics were never predictors.
Figure 1 summarises the design.

text.text: For each of five fixed salts, each patient was assigned by SHA-256(salt + patient identifier), using the first eight hexadecimal digits modulo 100.
Values of 80 to 99 formed the outer test set; values of 0 to 79 formed the development set, with a training role (0 to 59), tuning role (60 to 69) or calibration role (70 to 79).
A patient's role does not depend on the budget, and all cultures of a patient stay in that patient's role.
Development patients with at least one reported culture for the drug were ordered by a second salted hash for each budget sample.
A budget fraction of 10%, 25%, 50% or 100% took a prefix of this order, so budgets are nested within a sample.
Three budget samples were drawn for each fraction below 100%, and one at 100%, giving 15 planned analyses per fraction below 100% and 5 at 100% for each drug and model.
Rule-derived labels came only from development patients with the training role and were not limited by the budget.
Tuning, calibration and test patients never contributed rule-derived records.
Every method within an allocation used the same patients, and the outer test set was never resampled.
The same salts and cut points were applied at both sites; because the patients differ, the partitions themselves are site-specific.

Both model classes used fixed settings without tuning: L2-penalised logistic regression (C = 1, up to 1,000 iterations) and histogram gradient boosting (100 iterations, 7 leaves, at least 40 samples per leaf, L2 regularisation 5, no early stopping), as implemented in scikit-learn 1.8.0 [16].

text.text: One-hot encoding and standardisation were fitted on the training reported cultures of each allocation.
Sample weights were rescaled to a mean of 1.

The selected-weight and recalibrated methods use part of the budget for tuning or calibration, so they train on fewer reported labels than the all-budget baseline.
The allbudget comparison therefore measures the combined effect of adding rule-derived labels and of holding reported labels out for selection.
Recalibrated methods were also compared with the recalibrated reported-only model, so that both sides had the same calibration resources.
An analysis was unavailable if the training or test set had fewer than 10 positive or 10 negative cultures.
Weight selection required at least 5 of each class in tuning, and recalibration at least 10 of each in calibration.
On the outer test cultures we computed AUROC; average precision for the non-susceptible class (the AUPRC summary used here); Brier score [18]; log loss; observed prevalence; and mean predicted risk.

text.text: We also computed calibration-in-the-large (the intercept of a logistic model with logit p as offset; 0 ideal) and calibration slope (the coefficient of logit p; 1 ideal) [9].

text.text: Both calibration measures were fitted by unpenalised maximum likelihood and reported as missing when the fit did not converge or diverged.
Training and prediction times were recorded.
Stanford results were computed on a 2-CPU Linux container and UT Southwestern results in Google Colab, so runtimes are not comparable between sites.
For Brier-score differences we used a paired patient-cluster bootstrap [19] with 2,000 resamples.
text.formatted: For Brier-score differences we used a paired patient-cluster bootstrap <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19]</ref> with 2,000 resamples.

text.text: For each drug and outer split, one set of patient resamples was drawn and shared by every budget, sample, model and method.
All cultures of a drawn patient entered with that patient's multiplicity, and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicate differences formed the interval.
A positive difference means the compared method has a worse Brier score than its baseline.
These intervals describe uncertainty from test patients only.
They condition on the fitted models and do not include variation from budget sampling, training patients or refitting.
That variation is summarised separately across outer splits (median and range of split means) and budget samples.
The outer splits share patients, and the data had been explored in earlier analyses, so the splits are repeated exploratory evaluations, not independent replications.
Many comparisons were made without multiplicity adjustment.
Analyses were run with Python and pinned versions of numpy (2.3.5), pandas (2.2.3) and scikit-learn (1.8.0).
The Stanford results reported here come from the same notebook run on the same files as an earlier Colab run.
For the methods shared by both runs, test Brier scores agreed within 1.3 × 10 -8 and AUROC within 3.1 × 10 -5.

text.text: At Stanford, 16,197 cefepime, 29,973 cefoxitin and 37,222 ceftazidime reported cultures were included, with non-susceptibility of 4.5%, 11.8% and 7.9%.
Stanford released 36,420, 18,175 and 16,327 implied labels for these drugs, all susceptible.
At UT Southwestern, 19,759 cefepime cultures (1,208 non-susceptible; 6.1%) and 3,478 ceftazidime cultures (1,321 non-susceptible; 38.0%) were included.
The high ceftazidime prevalence is consistent with selective testing of that drug, but we did not investigate why it was tested.
The conservative heuristics produced 13,920 cefepime and 29,066 ceftazidime weak labels on cultures without a reported target result.
Only those from training-role patients entered training: in the first outer split, 8,423 and 17,535.
UT Southwestern ceftazidime test sets were small: in the first outer split, 711 cultures with 306 positives.
Supplementary Table S1 gives the budget allocation.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> gives the budget allocation.

text.text: At the 10% budget, the UT Southwestern ceftazidime budget contained a median of 274 reported cultures, with 31 tuning and 31 calibration cultures.
Table 3 summarises the UT Southwestern rule diagnostics.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref> summarises the UT Southwestern rule diagnostics.

text.text: Applying the rule text as written, rule predictions disagreed with 20 of 18,220 co-tested reported cefepime results and 75 of 2,210 ceftazidime results.
Under the conservative handling, which excluded 2,014 cultures where source antibiotics disagreed and 8 with conflicting source results, the figures were 16 of 16,690 and 17 of 1,553.
These counts describe a selected co-tested subset and are not error rates for the weak-label training pool.

Adding all rule-derived labels with equal weight lowered mean predicted risk well below the observed prevalence at both sites (Figure 2), most strongly at small budgets where rulederived records dominated the training data.
text.formatted: Adding all rule-derived labels with equal weight lowered mean predicted risk well below the observed prevalence at both sites (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), most strongly at small budgets where rulederived records dominated the training data.

text.text: For logistic regression at the 10% budget at Stanford, median mean predicted risk fell from 4.47% (reported only) to 0.35% (equal weight) for cefepime, from 12.21% to 2.88% for cefoxitin, and from 7.93% to 2.60% for ceftazidime.
Observed test prevalences were 4.85%, 11.92% and 8.12%.

At UT Southwestern the shift was larger for ceftazidime, from 35.0% to 0.42% against an observed 37.4%, because about 17,500 susceptible weak labels were added to a budget of a few hundred reported cultures.
The selected weight, class adjustment and prior correction largely removed this shift, and the all-budget baseline stayed close to the observed prevalence.
Table 4 and Figure 3 summarise Brier-score differences against the all-budget baseline, and Supplementary Table S2 gives the test metrics.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">4</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> summarise Brier-score differences against the all-budget baseline, and Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> gives the test metrics.

text.text: Equal-weight augmentation had a higher median Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary at both sites.
Its intervals lay above zero in 227 of 300 Stanford analyses and 191 of 200 UT Southwestern analyses, and never below zero.
At UT Southwestern ceftazidime the difference was large: a median of +0.127 at 10% for logistic regression, against a baseline Brier score of about 0.24.
The selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline.

Its median difference was positive in 38 of the 40 drug, model and budget summaries; the two exceptions were UT Southwestern ceftazidime at 10% (gradient boosting, -1.34 × 10 -3 ) and Stanford ceftazidime at 100% (logistic regression, -0.003 × 10 -3 ).

At the 10% budget the medians (× 10 -3 , logistic regression / gradient boosting) were +0.19 / +1.07 for Stanford cefepime, +0.41 / +1.12 for cefoxitin and +1.39 / +1.30 for ceftazidime, and +0.11 / +0.13 for UT Southwestern cefepime and +1.10 / -1.34 for ceftazidime.
Most individual intervals included zero.
Across all budgets, the intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5.
The direction varied between splits for UT Southwestern ceftazidime at 10%: for gradient boosting, 3 of 5 split means were below zero.
Results there were also unstable, with single analyses reaching +0.115 for logistic regression; the tuning sets in these analyses contained about 31 cultures.
Class adjustment and prior correction were also mostly worse than the all-budget baseline (Table 4).
text.formatted: Class adjustment and prior correction were also mostly worse than the all-budget baseline (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">4</ref>).

text.text: The tuning set often selected a weight of zero, which reproduces the reported-only model: in 146 of 296 Stanford analyses and 153 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses (Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: The tuning set often selected a weight of zero, which reproduces the reported-only model: in 146 of 296 Stanford analyses and 153 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S3</ref>).

text.text: For the selected weight, the comparison with the all-budget baseline then largely reflects the reported labels held out for tuning and calibration.
The all-budget baseline itself had a lower median Brier score than the reported-only model in every Stanford summary.
At UT Southwestern, differences between these two were small and mixed in sign.
Rule-derived labels changed AUROC little relative to the reported-only and all-budget models (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Rule-derived labels changed AUROC little relative to the reported-only and all-budget models (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: At Stanford, the median AUROC of logistic regression at the 100% budget was 0.70 for cefepime, 0.67 for cefoxitin and 0.71 for ceftazidime.
At UT Southwestern, the age-only models were close to chance: median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54 for cefepime and 0.49 to 0.53 for ceftazidime across budgets and methods.
The UT Southwestern comparisons are therefore informative mainly about calibration and the effect of class balance, not about ranking.
Recalibration was often unavailable at small budgets because calibration sets had too few positives.
For Stanford cefepime at 10%, the recalibrated reported-only model was available in 3 of 15 analyses and the recalibrated selected-weight comparison in 2 of 15.
Where both recalibrated models were available, their differences were usually exactly zero, because the tuning set had selected α = 0.
Remaining differences were small and of mixed sign (exported results).
Median training times per model at the 100% budget were below 0.4 s for every logistic regression method and below 0.35 s for gradient boosting methods without weight selection.
The selected weight required several fits (median 1.8 s for gradient boosting at Stanford).

At two sites, three antibiotics and two model classes, adding rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the entire reported-label budget for training.
Equal-weight augmentation was clearly worse, and the tuning-selected weight was usually slightly worse or indistinguishable.
These results do not show that rule-derived labels cannot help.
They show that, in this design, any benefit was not large enough to offset the reported labels set aside for weight selection, and that unweighted addition of single-class labels damaged calibration.

The result resembles Zhu et al.'s observation that clean validation data are often better spent on training [4], but the settings differ: tabular features, a small number of rules, labels that only ever imply the majority class, and probability-based evaluation.
text.formatted: The result resembles Zhu et al.'s observation that clean validation data are often better spent on training <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, but the settings differ: tabular features, a small number of rules, labels that only ever imply the majority class, and probability-based evaluation.

text.text: Our study does not test whether their conclusions hold generally.
It suggests that the comparison they recommend, against a model trained on all the clean labels, is also informative in this application.
Choosing α on a tuning set is a coarse form of the validation-guided reweighting studied by Ren et al. [5].
text.formatted: Choosing α on a tuning set is a coarse form of the validation-guided reweighting studied by Ren et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: That α = 0 was chosen in about half of the Stanford analyses and three-quarters of the UT Southwestern analyses indicates that the tuning sets often found no benefit from the rule-derived records.
The calibration findings agree with work on class-imbalance correction in risk prediction [7, 8].
text.formatted: The calibration findings agree with work on class-imbalance correction in risk prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Adding many susceptible labels acts like oversampling the majority class, and the resulting underestimation of risk could largely be undone by restoring the reported class proportions, either through weights or through a prior correction [11].
text.formatted: Adding many susceptible labels acts like oversampling the majority class, and the resulting underestimation of risk could largely be undone by restoring the reported class proportions, either through weights or through a prior correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: These corrections recovered calibration-in-the-large but not the Brier score of the all-budget baseline.
A likely contributor is that rule-derived cultures differ from reported cultures in more than class proportion, violating the label-shift assumption [10].
text.formatted: A likely contributor is that rule-derived cultures differ from reported cultures in more than class proportion, violating the label-shift assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: We did not test this directly.
Weak-label quality is uncertain at both sites.
Stanford's implied labels follow documented laboratory protocols [12], but we know of no independent validation of their accuracy.
text.formatted: Stanford's implied labels follow documented laboratory protocols <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, but we know of no independent validation of their accuracy.

text.text: At UT Southwestern, the labels are our own application of Stanford rule text.

Agreement with reported results was high on co-tested cultures (for example, 16 disagreements among 16,690 cefepime cultures), but those cultures were selected for testing and may not represent the cultures that received weak labels.
Our check on Stanford data also showed that the rule text alone does not reproduce Stanford's released labels.
WRENCH highlighted that weak-label sources differ in ways that complicate comparison [2].
text.formatted: WRENCH highlighted that weak-label sources differ in ways that complicate comparison <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: The same applies here: the two sites differ in how labels were produced as well as in patients, testing practice and features.
The two-site design should not be read as external validation.
Following the distinction drawn in prediction-model research [14], we did not take a model fitted at Stanford and evaluate it at UT Southwestern.
text.formatted: Following the distinction drawn in prediction-model research <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref>, we did not take a model fitted at Stanford and evaluate it at UT Southwestern.

text.text: We repeated the design and refitted every model at each site.
The primary feature sets differ (rich at Stanford, age-only at UT Southwestern), and the UT Southwestern models had almost no discrimination.
The UT Southwestern results therefore test whether the label-budget findings recur under weaker features and differently built labels, not whether a particular model transports.
We also could not verify whether the two datasets share patients.

Strengths include a design in which every method uses the same reported patients within an allocation; an explicit all-budget baseline; separate tuning and calibration patients; paired cluster bootstrap intervals; reporting of availability, including analyses that could not be run; and checks that a selected weight of zero reproduces the reported-only model exactly.
The limitations are substantial.
The analysis is exploratory, and the Stanford data had been examined in earlier analyses with the same outer splits, so there is no untouched confirmatory test set.
Outer splits overlap, and we made many comparisons without adjustment.
Bootstrap intervals cover only test-patient sampling.
Reported results may be affected by selective testing and are not assumed to be error-free; the UT Southwestern ceftazidime prevalence of 38% suggests strong selection.
The timing of resistance-history records is not verified, so leakage of information unavailable at prediction time cannot be excluded at Stanford.
Dates are jittered, so no temporal validation was attempted.
The budgets were simulated by subsampling fully labelled data, and real low-label settings may differ in which cultures are labelled.
Hyperparameters were fixed.
The rules imply only susceptibility.
The study does not assess clinical utility, and nothing here supports clinical use of these models or rules.
A preliminary feature-matched comparison between sites was not part of the completed analyses and is not reported.

Useful next steps are a prespecified analysis on data not used during method development; feature sets that are matched across sites where meanings can be established; weak-label sources that can imply both classes; and an independent assessment of rule validity at each laboratory.
Any new method for combining weak and reported labels should be compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline and evaluated on calibration as well as discrimination.

In exploratory label-budget experiments at two sites, rule-derived susceptibility labels did not consistently improve probability prediction compared with using the whole reported-label budget for training, and unweighted addition of these single-class labels seriously miscalibrated predictions.
Evaluations of weak supervision should count the reported labels used for tuning and calibration, include an all-budget reported-only baseline, and report calibration alongside discrimination.

text.text: Reported-label budget and its allocation: patients / cultures / non-susceptible cultures, median across outer splits and budget samples.
Figure 1.
Design of one allocation.
Within an allocation, every method uses the same patients, and test patients are never used for fitting, preprocessing, weight selection or recalibration.
The all-budget baseline trains one model on the budgeted training, tuning and calibration reported labels together.
Figure 2.
Mean predicted risk on the outer test set by reported-label budget (logistic regression).
Each point is the median across outer splits of the split mean over budget samples.
Hollow points rest on fewer analyses than planned and are not joined to neighbouring points.
Dotted line: observed prevalence (median across splits).
Figure 3.
Brier-score difference (× 10 -3 ) between each rule-derived method and the all-budget reported-only baseline; positive values mean the rule-derived method is worse.
Point: median across outer splits of the split mean over budget samples; bar: range across outer splits.
Hollow points rest on fewer analyses than planned.
Equal-weight results are in Table 4; their scale would hide the other methods.
Note the different y-axis scales.
Figure 4.
AUROC by reported-label budget (logistic regression).
Line: median across outer splits of the split mean; band: range across outer splits; hollow points rest on fewer analyses than planned.
Dotted line: AUROC 0.5.
Analysis cohorts.
Rule-derived cultures: released implied labels (Stanford) or conservative research heuristics (UT Southwestern), excluding cultures with a reported target result.
Training rule-derived cultures and test counts are for the first outer split.
UT Southwestern rule diagnostics.
Disagreement = rule predicts susceptible, reported result nonsusceptible, among cultures with both.
Brier-score difference between rule-derived methods and the all-budget reported-only baseline, × 10 -3 (positive = rule-derived method worse).
Each cell: median across analyses (minimum to maximum); number of 95% paired bootstrap intervals above zero / below zero / including zero.
Planned analyses: 15 at 10%, 5 at 100%; fewer are noted.
LR, logistic regression; HGB, histogram gradient boosting.
